common_name: Tsumugi Shibori Fatsia (Tie-Dyed White-Speckled Japanese Aralia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade, sheltered from wind and hot sun; Tsumugi Shibori is slower to establish and slightly less hardy than the plain green species.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade, sheltered from harsh wind and hot midday sun. Tsumugi Shibori is the old Japanese variegated seed strain — its name means tie-dyed cloth — from which the better-known 'Spider's Web' was later selected, bearing glossy, deeply lobed leaves heavily speckled and dusted with white flecking that can spread across much of the leaf, with new growth sometimes emerging nearly all white before greening. It is slower growing and somewhat less cold-hardy than the plain green species, so give it a sheltered site and extra winter protection at the cold edge of its range.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this subtropical island endemic is less cold-hardy than the related Fatsia japonica and needs a sheltered, near frost-free site.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, in a sheltered site protected from hard frost. Native to Japan's subtropical Bonin (Ogasawara) Islands, this close relative of Fatsia japonica shares the same bold, glossy, deeply lobed palmate foliage and architectural form but has less coarsely toothed leaf lobes and is noticeably less cold-hardy, limiting it to the mildest shaded gardens or large containers that can be moved under cover in winter. Small clusters of white flowers followed by dark berries appear on mature plants, and it needs only occasional pruning to remove damaged or overly long stems.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade; give it a sheltered woodland-edge position out of harsh winter wind.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade beneath open tree canopy, in a site sheltered from harsh winter wind. This large Himalayan species carries bold, glossy, pinnately divided evergreen leaves with up to 15 narrow, spiny leaflets, producing spreading sprays of yellow flowers in early to mid-spring followed by blue-black, powder-coated berries. It is one of the parent species behind some Mahonia x media hybrids and needs only occasional pruning to remove dead or leggy canes.

common_name: Maharajah Nepal Mahonia (Deep-Yellow Himalayan Winter Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade; Maharajah is a large, open, upright selection valued for unusually deep-yellow flowers.

directions: Plant in moist but well-drained, humus-rich soil in full to partial shade. Maharajah is a large, open, upright selection of the Himalayan Mahonia napaulensis with glossy, dark green leaves made up of about 15 narrow, spiny leaflets, producing spreading sprays of deep yellow flowers in early to mid-spring followed by blue-black, powder-coated berries. It is currently included in an ongoing Royal Horticultural Society trial evaluating Mahonia cultivars; prune only to remove dead or damaged canes.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to full shade; this Chinese species tolerates a wider range of light than most mahonias.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in full sun to full shade — this Chinese species tolerates a wide range of light levels better than many mahonias. Native to forest, scrub, and hillside sites in Yunnan, Sichuan, and neighboring regions, it is a bold shrub to about 10 feet tall with large, pinnately divided evergreen leaves and racemes of richly fragrant, yellow to orange-yellow flowers in early spring, followed by blue-black berries. Its leaves have a long history of use in traditional Chinese medicine; prune only to remove dead or leggy canes.

common_name: Ken Hartman Shasta Mahonia (Bronze-New-Growth California Holly Grape)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained soil; Ken Hartman tolerates sun to mostly shade once established and needs only low to moderate water.

directions: Site in well-drained soil in anything from sun to mostly shade, where this erect, compact selection of the California native Mahonia pinnata forms a dense 4-5 foot evergreen mound. Its glossy, spiny-toothed pinnate leaves emerge bronzy-orange before maturing to dark green, and bright yellow flowers in spring are followed by blue berries that draw birds, bees, and butterflies. It is drought tolerant once established and needs only occasional removal of dead or crossing canes.

common_name: Cosmo Crawl Oregon Grape (Prostrate Creeping Mahonia)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or spring in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Cosmo Crawl is a particularly prostrate, suckering selection.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Cosmo Crawl spreads by suckers into a low, dense groundcover rather than growing upright like typical Oregon grape. Its extremely glossy, spiny-toothed leaflets turn reddish-purple in winter cold, and dense clusters of bright yellow flowers open in spring, followed by blue-black berries that attract birds. It is drought tolerant once established and makes a useful low-maintenance bank or slope cover; shear lightly if needed to keep it tidy.
